stimulus.text:
“The essential and direct End of the present defensive alliance is to maintain effectually the liberty, Sovereignty, and independance absolute and unlimited of the said united States, as well in Matters of Gouvernement as of commerce.”
—Treaty of Alliance between the United States and France, Article 2, February 6, 1778 (spelling as in the original)
stimulus.source_note: Treaty of Alliance between the United States and France, February 6, 1778. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Treaty of Alliance, February 6, 1778, public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.5 The American Revolution, A. The War for Independence

primary_sources: Treaty of Alliance between the United States and France (1778)

stem: France signed this treaty in February 1778, rather than in 1776, most directly because

options.text: Congress had already won the war without foreign help
options.misconception: The war was far from won in early 1778; it went on for five more years, until 1783.

options.text: Spain had forced France to join the war
options.misconception: Spain did not force France into the alliance; France acted from its own wish to weaken Britain, and Spain joined later.

options.text: The American victory at Saratoga convinced France to ally
The British navy had been destroyed at Yorktown
options.misconception: Yorktown came in 1781, three years after the treaty; no British fleet was destroyed there in 1778.

rationales.C: France sent secret aid before 1778 but waited for proof the Americans could win; Saratoga supplied it, and the treaty followed within months.
rationales.D: Yorktown was in 1781, three years after the treaty, so it cannot explain a decision made in 1778.
rationales.A: The war was not won in 1778; it lasted until 1783, and American victory needed French help.
rationales.B: France chose the alliance to weaken Britain, its old enemy; Spain joined the war later, on its own terms.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what France was waiting for. Before 1778 France sent secret supplies, but it would not risk open war with Britain for a losing cause.
2. Ask what changed its mind. Saratoga destroyed a British army and showed the Americans could win in the field.
3. Check the dates. Yorktown, Spanish entry, and victory all came later, so none of them explains February 1778.
Remember: allies join winners — ask what proof of winning came just before the signature. Background: France had sent covert arms and supplies before 1778 but no open aid.
